visible.summary:
Myanmar is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Section 377 of the Penal Code criminalises same-sex intimacy, and police use “shadow laws” — notably Section 30(d) of the Rangoon Police Act, allowing detention of anyone who cannot “satisfactorily account” for themselves — to target trans and gender-nonconforming people. Since the February 2021 coup the situation has turned lethal: the National Unity Government documented 17 LGBT people killed by mid-2022, and rights groups document arrests, torture, and sexual abuse of LGBT people by junta authorities, with the 2024 Conscription Law falling brutally on queer people.

In 2025 the junta banned seven books for LGBTQ+ content as “obscene.” There is no legal gender recognition, no protection of any kind, and no institutional recourse — police and military are the primary predators. Resistance-controlled areas are nominally friendlier but are active war zones.

For a visitor: any visible gender nonconformity risks detention under police-act powers, with torture documented in custody; the general security collapse compounds everything.
visible.tangentialFactors: Section 377 criminalises same-sex intimacy — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners; the police-act "shadow law" is the trans-specific detention mechanism.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: General civil-war risks affect all travelers and are out of scope; the score reflects trans-specific persecution by the junta.

sources.claim: Outright International overview (updated March 2026): Section 377 used to detain people who cannot 'satisfactorily account' for their presence; after the 1 Feb 2021 coup risks intensified — torture/sexual violence in detention, Oct 2022 Organization Registration Law (prison terms for NGO non-compliance), compulsory military service announced Feb 2024, seven LGBTQ-themed books banned 2025. Verdict: avoid entirely.

DVB (Jan 2024): post-coup authorities commit attacks, arrest, torture and sexual abuse against LGBT people; the NUG recorded 17 LGBT killed and 2 critically injured since 1 Feb 2021; 'Rainbow Amid the Storm' found 50% of LGBT respondents have no confidence in the legal system and 68%+ fear repercussions from abusers.

Human Rights Myanmar submission (June 2024) to the UN Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial executions: killing of LGBTIQ+ persons in military-controlled Myanmar - 5 to 12 individuals dead since the coup; Section 377 enforcement intensified as an aggravating factor; militarised policing, arbitrary detention and vague public-decency laws endanger the right to life.

RFA (10 Jan 2025): junta banned seven named LGBTQ-themed books as 'obscene' with prosecutions announced for publishers; colonial-era law carries up to 10 years for gay sex; LGBTQ+ people hit hard since the Feb 2021 coup.

ASEAN SOGIE Caucus (March 2025, from Queers of Burma Alternative research Jan 2025): the 2024 Conscription Law drives queer people into fear and displacement; Section 377 carries life imprisonment or up to 10 years, and 1945 Police Act s.35(c) (face covering, up to 3 months) is used specifically against transgender people.

Guardian (2 Feb 2016): Colors Rainbow's work in Yangon — trans woman Nat Nat We describes arrest, stripping, a beating and 14 days' detention for walking home at night, with police accusing her of sex work; documents routine police violence against trans women.

Washington Blade (2 Nov 2018): Aung Myo Htut (aka Addy Chen), an outspoken HIV-positive LGBTI advocate and Yangon restaurant owner, was charged under Penal Code 377 over an alleged offence against an employee — Section 377 in active use, with the community demanding fair media coverage.

HuffPost (17 Oct 2015): colonial-era criminalisation; 2013 Mandalay arrests of trans women forced to strip and parade naked while photographed (police called it a 'public service'); nat kadaws (spirit mediums) are culturally visible transgender women — visibility coexisting with criminalisation.

visible.summary:
Cuba is workable for trans visitors — one of Latin America's most legally transformed countries. The 2019 Constitution bans discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity; the 2022 Family Code (66.87% referendum approval) overhauled family law; and trans people can change legal gender — the July 2025 civil-registry reform further eliminated bureaucratic hurdles for name changes. CENESEX, the state sex-education centre, runs an official trans-care programme, and Havana has a visible, state-tolerated trans community.

The counterweights are systemic rather than trans-specific: Cuba is a one-party state with no independent civil society, arbitrary-detention powers are broad, the economic crisis has degraded healthcare (hormone availability is unreliable), and police discretion is wide. There is no documented pattern of police targeting trans people as trans — the historical UMAP camps era is long past and officially repudiated — but there is also no independent recourse if something goes wrong.

For a visitor: no legal exposure for gender expression or documents; low street-hostility in tourist areas; the risk is the general absence of rule-of-law recourse.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2022 Family Code overhauled family law (including same-sex marriage) — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
visible.localsOnly: The civil-registry LGR reform, CENESEX trans-care programme, and unreliable hormone availability are resident-facing.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Political repression, shortages, and detention powers affect all travelers; LGR mechanics are resident-facing.

sources.claim: LegalClarity overview (30 May 2026): documents Cuba's arc from the UMAP forced-labour camps for gay men (1965-68, ~60 hrs/week cutting cane in Camagüey, electric-shock and injection 'curing' experiments) to today's progressive framework — 1979 Penal Code removal of consensual same-sex acts, Castro's public acceptance of blame (La Jornada, 2010), Resolution 126 (2008) trans healthcare in the public system, the 2019 Constitution (Art 42, first to name sexual orientation and gender identity as protected categories), and the 2022 Family Code (same-sex marriage/adoption, legal gender change without surgery). Notes the gap between law and daily life: Labor Code Law 116 bars SOGI discrimination but does not list gender identity as a separate protected ground, and the Labor Code's article 2(b) covers orientation, not identity.

Americas Quarterly (15 Sept 2022): previews Cuba's 25 Sept 2022 Family Code referendum — only the 4th national vote since 1959 — which would guarantee marriage equality, surrogacy, codified domestic-violence penalties and shared parental rights; opponents cite religious objections and fear child-welfare provisions could be used against dissidents, while some government opponents planned to vote No purely to deny the Díaz-Canel administration a win amid the post-July-2021 crackdown (1,400+ arrestees) and record emigration. Useful context for how contested (rather than state-enforced) the equality settlement is.

Links International Journal of Socialist Renewal (23 Dec 2011): sympathetic first-person account 'Rainbow Cuba' disputing claims of systematic state homophobia — documents the UMAP camps (conscripts paid seven pesos a day), the 1975 declaration-era turning point, and CENESEX's state-backed programme: a trans-rights campaign, work with the police and the supreme court, and sexual-diversity education. Historical baseline (pre-2019 constitution) showing official institutions campaigning for LGBT acceptance since the late 2000s.

Washington Blade (21 Dec 2013): Cuban lawmakers approved a labor-law amendment banning employment discrimination on sexual orientation after intense parliamentary debate; Mariela Castro (CENESEX) proposed extending it to gender identity, disability and HIV status — the trans-specific amendment drew support from some Christian and intellectual legislators but the report makes clear passage of the SOGI ban was the confirmed outcome. Predates the 2019 Constitution/2022 Family Code (superseded in scope, not in error).

Washington Blade (26 May 2018): documents Cuba's use of 'treason'/'treason against the homeland' charges against LGBTI citizens who flee to seek asylum — Victor Manuel Dueñas and Onasis Torres faced up to 8 years in prison if they returned after filing Dutch asylum claims (Jan 2018); a woman deported from the Netherlands was detained (19 May 2018), and LGBTI activists (incl. Nelson Gandulla, Cuban LGBTI Equality Foundation) remained monitored. Relevant to visitors: Cuba's hostility toward emigration/asylum, not toward gender expression as such.

visible.summary:
Jamaica is dangerous for trans visitors. The Offences Against the Person Act (buggery law, up to 10 years) remains on the books and shapes police culture; there is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection. The defining case is Dwayne Jones, a gender-nonconforming 16-year-old beaten, stabbed, and shot to death by a mob at a 2013 street party after being outed — whose killing police failed to investigate, now the subject of an Inter-American Commission case (Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica) documenting state failure to protect trans life.

Police harassment of trans women is documented in the public-health literature, and mob justice against perceived LGBT people remains a live risk — community members report that violence against trans people (beatings, stonings) is common but rarely reported because there is no point. Tourist resorts (Montego Bay, Negril, Ocho Rios) are heavily insulated bubbles where incidents are rare, but a visibly trans visitor outside them faces real outing-violence risk with indifferent police.
visible.tangentialFactors: The buggery law (up to 10 years) is a formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners and shapes police culture.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: The buggery law is a situational/climate factor; resort vs. non-resort risk differs sharply.

sources.claim: Amicus brief in Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica before the Inter-American Commission (filed Feb 2024): argues Jamaica's continued criminalisation of LGBTQ persons and systemic discrimination make transgender persons especially vulnerable — sections document housing insecurity, educational and employment insecurity for transgender Jamaicans under the discrimination regime.

UNDP 'Being LGBT in Jamaica' National Survey (March 2023): national survey of LGBT Jamaicans with dedicated chapters on violence due to prejudice and discrimination and on transgender access to health care; quantifies lived experience of violence and service exclusion under the criminalisation backdrop.

US DOJ/EOIR Jamaica country packet (2013): Offences Against the Person Act makes 'buggery' punishable by up to 10 years' hard labour; LGBT victims are reluctant to report because police leak incident details, fail to investigate LGBT violence including murder, and do not intervene during attacks (documented via the CVC and local organisations).

IACHR Report on the Situation of Human Rights in Jamaica (10 Aug 2012): finds 'the violent persecution and fear to which gays and lesbians are subject in Jamaica to be deplorable'; covers citizen security, police killings including the May 2010 operation, and justice administration, with civil-society input from Jamaicans for Justice and the Jamaica Forum for Lesbians, All-Sexuals and Gays (J-FLAG).

HRW letter (30 Nov 2004) citing its report 'Hated to Death: Homophobia, Violence, and Jamaica's HIV/AIDS Epidemic': documents police harassment of gay men and HIV/AIDS outreach workers, community and family violence carried out with impunity, and official indifference; five Jamaican human-rights organisations backed the report's 16 Nov 2004 Kingston launch.

Amnesty International urgent appeal (4 Jun 2006): reports vigilante violence and police ill-treatment or torture of LGBT people in Jamaica — gay men and lesbians beaten, cut, burned, raped and shot once orientation known; lesbians raped and driven into asylum abroad; concern that prominent musicians promote homophobia.

visible.summary:
Trinidad and Tobago demands real caution from trans visitors — legally improved, socially dangerous. The courts struck down the colonial buggery laws (Jones v. AG, 2018, upheld on appeal), removing criminalisation of same-sex intimacy; but there is no legal gender recognition, no SOGI anti-discrimination protection, and parliament has repeatedly rejected reforms (the ruling party's constitution review again refused SOGI protections in 2024).

Documented street risk is substantial: community advocates report trans people are still “beaten, stoned and chopped,” with most incidents never reported; and police have publicly warned of a spate of Grindr ambush robberies — criminals using fake profiles to lure LGBT victims to meetings followed by armed robbery (multiple cases through 2023-2024, including a Cocorite man beaten and robbed). This dating-app predation pattern is a direct traveler concern.
visible.tangentialFactors: The Grindr ambush robbery pattern is a direct risk for trans visitors using apps.
visible.localsOnly: No LGR and no SOGI anti-discrimination protection — resident-facing; the “beaten, stoned and chopped” pattern describes residents.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Decriminalisation status and reform rejections are climate/legal context; no trans-specific statute exists.

sources.claim: Trinidad and Tobago Newsday (July 2024): 'Long way yet for recognition, safe spaces' - TT Transgender Coalition director Rae Alibey says the trans community is the most marginalised and not even recognised in T&T; gender identity is not recognised separately from sexual orientation; gender-identity markers on institutional forms are absent; national discussions and attitudinal research needed.

Newsday (Nov 2024): police warning over cyber criminals - Grindr hook-ups ending in cars, cash and phones stolen; criminals create fake dating accounts to lure LGBT+ victims into meetings followed by armed robbery, beatings or sexual assault; two separate incidents reported in one week.

Newsday editorial (June 2024): 'Grind hate to a halt' - a spate of Grindr-related attacks (almost half a dozen in recent months); Supt Claire Guy-Alleyne points to gaps in the law: 'We don't have a specific hate crime category in legislation'; the editorial argues the gap must be closed.

CNC3 (23 Aug 2024): the PNM Constitution Review Committee rejected adding sexual-orientation protections to the national constitution (decision announced at a special convention); CAISO's Dr Angelique Nixon said the community has 'been waiting far too long for equal rights and protection'. Documents LGBTQ-rights exclusion from the 2024 constitutional-review process.

GlobalGayz (Aug 2012): travel/culture profile stating that although homosexuality is illegal 'the laws are mostly ignored' in practice; describes tourist-facing social scene and island context. Usable as a 2012 non-enforcement baseline; predates the 2018 decriminalisation ruling, so dated for current-law purposes.

PinkNews (21 Nov 2017): first-person appeal by activist Jason Jones during his High Court challenge to T&T's same-sex criminalisation — he faces up to 25 years' imprisonment for consensual sex with an adult male partner; article carries the litigation campaign. Marks the constitutional challenge that put the criminal law in play.

Erasing 76 Crimes (23 Jun 2016): PM Keith Rowley told Parliament (17 Jun 2016) the state must protect all citizens 'regardless of whom they sleep with', while refusing to repeal the same-sex criminal laws; cites Newsday. Documents the reform-refusal gap in official rhetoric as of 2016.

visible.summary:
Ghana is dangerous for trans visitors — and narrowly avoided becoming much worse. In February 2024 parliament unanimously passed the Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill: up to 3 years in prison for simply identifying as LGBT, and 5 years for “promotion.” President Akufo-Addo refused to assent pending legal challenges, the Supreme Court dismissed the challenges in December 2024, and the bill lapsed when the 8th parliament dissolved — but its unanimous passage and broad public support signal the political climate, and reintroduction is expected.

Under existing law, “unnatural carnal knowledge” carries up to 3 years, and mob justice against perceived LGBT people is documented. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection. Accra has a resilient underground community (LGBT+ Rights Ghana — whose 2021 office opening was raided and shut down within weeks), but nothing that can protect a visitor.
visible.tangentialFactors: “Unnatural carnal knowledge” (up to 3 years) criminalises same-sex conduct — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners; the lapsed bill would have criminalised identity itself.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: The 2024 bill never became law (lapsed unassented); its significance is climate/trajectory.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Feb 2024) covers Ghana's parliament passing the anti-LGBT bill.

Human Rights Watch (5 Mar 2024): called on Ghana's president to veto the anti-LGBT bill — the page's call to 'veto the bill' is readable; bill sharply increased penalties and criminalised advocacy (bill itself later lapsed — see superseded note on the BBC/JURIST entries).

BBC: Ghana's Supreme Court unanimously dismissed two challenges to the anti-LGBT bill — Justice Avril Lovelace-Johnson: 'Until there's presidential assent, there is no act', review deferred until the president signs; petitioners' lawyers said they would explore options. SUPERSEDED: Ghana's 2024 anti-LGBTQ 'Human Sexuality' bill lapsed unsigned when Parliament dissolved pre-2024 election; colonial 'unnatural carnal knowledge' criminalisation persists; Pres. Mahama signalled willingness to sign a reintroduced bill

JURIST (Feb 2024): Parliament passed the Promotion of Proper Human Sexual Rights and Ghanaian Family Values Bill 2021 unanimously after its third reading — up to 3 years for identifying as LGBTQ+, up to 5 years for forming or funding LGBTQ+ groups. SUPERSEDED: Ghana's 2024 anti-LGBTQ 'Human Sexuality' bill lapsed unsigned when Parliament dissolved pre-2024 election; colonial 'unnatural carnal knowledge' criminalisation persists; Pres. Mahama signalled willingness to sign a reintroduced bill

HRW report (Jan 2018) 'No Choice but to Deny Who I Am': full PDF - violence and discrimination against LGBT people in Ghana; section 104(1)(b) criminalises 'unnatural carnal knowledge' but is rarely enforced; documents mob violence, police abuse, and extortion.

HRW report landing page (8 Jan 2018), 'No Choice but to Deny Who I Am: Violence and Discrimination against LGBT People in Ghana' — full report and annex downloads; endnotes document 2017 victim interviews (Kumasi, Tamale) and police/vigilante violence.

Bachelor thesis (Diaconia University of Applied Sciences, Helsinki, 2017) by Seree Yeboa-Mensa: survey of 113 Ghanaians living in Finland on LGBT rights in Ghana - most opposed decriminalisation/legalisation, citing religio-cultural reasons and effects on children; most supported families loving and accepting LGBT members but not blessing their marriages.

visible.summary:
Morocco is dangerous for trans visitors. Article 489 criminalises same-sex “indecent acts” (6 months–3 years), and Cairo 52 documents that trans people face de-facto criminalisation under Article 498 morality provisions — arrests based on gender-expression discrepancies and forced outing. The 2026 Cairo 52 report “A Web of Violence” describes a legal-medical-social system of erasure for trans people, including a de facto prohibition on transition care.

Visitor-relevant cases exist: in 2024, Brazilian influencer Liziane Gutierrez was arrested in Marrakesh, accused by police of being transgender, and alleges she was forced to show her genitals — she spent a month in jail. In 2019, Marrakesh police filmed and humiliated a cross-dressing man after a traffic accident, leaking the video online. There is no LGR framework and police have wide discretion; tourist areas (Marrakesh, Agadir) are more tolerant in practice but the legal exposure is constant.

The Gutierrez case demonstrates that even a cisgender visitor suspected of being trans can face genital inspection and jail.
visible.tangentialFactors: Article 489 criminalises same-sex “indecent acts” (6 months–3 years) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners.
visible.localsOnly: The de facto transition-care prohibition described in Cairo 52's "A Web of Violence" is resident-facing.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is a situational/climate factor; the 2024 Gutierrez arrest was officially for filming a policeman — the trans-suspicion genital inspection is her allegation, disputed by Morocco.

sources.claim: Cairo 52 report 'A Web of Violence: The Systemic Erasure of Transgender People in Morocco' (Jan 2026, by Hamzawya and Nora Noralla): based on interviews with 17 trans and non-binary Moroccans - documents an interlocking system of legal, medical, social and economic hostility; Morocco once pioneered gender-affirming surgery for foreigners but now enforces a de facto prohibition for its own citizens; Article 489 weaponised to arrest trans people based on gender expression; no legal gender recognition pathway.

Cairo 52 country review of Morocco: no specific provisions on transition, but de facto criminalisation under Article 498 (moral charges, gender-expression discrepancies, involuntary outing); no gender-affirming healthcare framework, leading some to self-medicate; a 2021 recognition process exists for intersex people only; the Grand Mufti opposes transition.
Hindustan Times (Nov 2024): an Instagram model alleges Moroccan police forced her to show her genitals over trans suspicions - reported police abuse of a trans woman based on appearance.

El País (Jan 2019): Moroccan police subjected a Marrakesh cross-dresser to online humiliation - after a minor traffic accident, Chafiq was handcuffed and filmed by bystanders and police officers, who also photographed his ID documents and posted them online; he sought asylum in Europe. Homosexuality is punishable in Morocco.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Article 489 criminalises 'indecent acts' between persons of the same sex (6 months to 3 years) with wide police discretion and arbitrary arrests; 170 people charged with same-sex relations in 2018; HRW documented a 2020 campaign of online harassment of presumed gay and bisexual men; no legal gender recognition; public identification as LGBTIQ carries significant risk of violence and harassment; authorities block LGBTIQ organisations.

HRW report (April 2018) 'Audacity in Adversity': LGBT activism in the Middle East and North Africa - includes Morocco's Article 489 criminalisation and the annex of laws used to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression across MENA.
ILGA 'State-Sponsored Homophobia' (May 2008, Daniel Ottosson): world survey of laws prohibiting same-sex activity between consenting adults - country-by-country legal survey including Morocco.
Washington Blade (Sept 2014): the UN Human Rights Council adopted the SOGI resolution - international context for human-rights scrutiny of countries including Morocco.
